correctness.rationale: Every proper ideal of a finite local ring with \(J^2=0\) is exactly one residue-field subspace of J. Any two proper ideals have product zero. Counting the only nonzero k-tuples gives \(1-[1+k(S-1)]/(S+1)^k\), with S the Gaussian subspace count. Elementary exact inequalities give the sole nonfield field-value equality \((q,d,k)=(2,2,2)\), plus the full sign profile. An explicit six-ideal ring has 27 zero-product pairs out of 36. The classification of commutative rings of sizes four and six proves least order eight. Independently enumerated ideal tables and direct products in two eight-element rings and four smaller nonfields agree with all counts; no extrapolation is needed.

originality.rationale: The accessible full text of arXiv:2608.14618 explicitly conjectures in Conjecture 4.2 that the ideal-product probability \(1-2^{-k}\) characterizes fields for each \(k\ge2\). Its detailed examples and formulas cover fields, Boolean, chain and principal ideal rings, not the nonprincipal square-zero local example. The example of order eight contradicts the statement for \(k=2\) and the all-k family theorem gives a new exact equality boundary. Exact-equivalence searches of published mathematical records, current literature, and accessible prior-claim titles revealed no equivalent statement. Priority is best knowledge, not a global proof of nonexistence.

value.rationale: The result falsifies a specific published field-characterization conjecture and proves that its smallest nonfield counterexample has eight elements, a sharp substantive boundary. The all-k classification covers every finite local square-zero commutative ring, including nonsplit and mixed-characteristic examples. It also gives a strict three-regime comparison with the field benchmark: one-generator radicals cross after three factors, multidimensional radicals dominate, and the unique collision is at \((q,d,k)=(2,2,2)\). This is a natural complete family calculation motivated by an explicit literature gap, not arbitrary recomputation of a known table.
